## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 2/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules.

## Claim under review
"Rainbow-style colormaps (jet) create false features: bright bands read as local maxima even where the underlying data value is lower, so jet misleads viewers with AND without CVD — a documented failure mode, not a style preference."

**Source:** https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0199239 (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "An example of how the data may be misinterpreted are evident in the bright yellow spots in (b) and (c), which appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) and dark yellow (in c) actually represent the highest values."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

content.content:
# Analysis of Figure 1 and Colormap Specifications

## Full Surrounding Paragraph

"An example of how the data may be misinterpreted are evident in the bright yellow spots in (b) and (c), which appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) and dark yellow (in c) actually represent the highest values. For someone who is red-green colorblind, this is made even more difficult to interpret due to the broad, bright band in the center of the colormap with values that are difficult to distinguish."

## Figure 1 Caption

"Comparison between different colormaps overlaid onto the test image by Kovesi and a nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry image. Colormaps are as follows: (a) perceptually uniform grayscale, (b) jet, (c) jet as it appears to someone with red-green colorblindness, and (d) viridis."

## Critical Finding

**Panel (b) shows jet under normal vision; panel (c) shows a CVD simulation.** The caption explicitly states: "(c) jet as it appears to someone with red-green colorblindness."

## Jet Misleading Normal Vision

The paper notes that problematic colormaps "can cause misinterpretation for certain types of data, even for those with normal color vision." The "bright yellow spots" in panel (b)—the normal vision rendering—appear to represent higher values than they actually do, demonstrating that jet is inherently misleading regardless of CVD status.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Borland and Taylor's "Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful":

## Publication Details

The rainbow color map has been formally "considered harmful" in the visualization research literature since at least 2007, when Borland and Taylor laid out the case in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications.

## Main Arguments

According to Borland and Taylor, "The rainbow color map confuses viewers through its lack of perceptual ordering, obscures data through its uncontrolled luminance variation, and actively misleads interpretation through the introduction of non-data-dependent gradients."

The paper identifies three key problems:

1. **Non-monotonic luminance**: A good color scale should have equal steps in the data look like equal steps in color, but the rainbow fails this badly—it races through some regions with almost no visible change and then lurches at others with tiny changes in value snapping between colors.

2. **False boundaries and confusing ordering**: The rainbow puts boundaries in the data visualization that the data itself did not contain. Bright stripes in the rainbow falsely suggest segmented regions that have no such boundaries in reality.

3. **Practical impact on data interpretation**: When researchers tested how physicians read artery visualizations, those using a rainbow color scheme took longer to reach a diagnosis and made significantly more errors than those using a perceptually designed scale.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

# Summary of Ware, Stone & Szafir's Argument

Based on the webpage content provided, the authors **concede** that rainbow colormaps have real problems, including luminance-related issues. The article states:

> "The rainbow colormap used here has all the usual problems: it's not uniform in its luminance (brightness)"

However, they **reframe the practical significance** of these flaws. Rather than disputing that false features occur, they argue these issues are often not relevant to actual real-world tasks. As the piece notes:

> "One commonly cited issue is that because luminance changes back and forth across the scale, it is impossible to read shape from a visualization"

Yet they suggest this criticism is largely a "strawman" for common mapping applications.

**Regarding empirical evidence:** The article does not indicate they dispute the evidence base for rainbow problems. Instead, it highlights research showing rainbows have *advantages* for specific tasks—particularly "reading a value off a map using a key" and drawing attention to global structure.

Their core position, quoted directly from the paper:

> "We understand well enough why rainbows can be bad; let us focus instead on finding out when and why they are good."

They accept the established critiques but advocate shifting focus toward identifying appropriate contexts for rainbow use.

I found the paper you were looking for. Here's the information about this research:

Crameri, F., G.E. Shephard, and P.J. Heron published "The misuse of colour in science communication" in Nature Communications, volume 11, article 5444, in 2020.

The paper addresses several key issues:

**Main Problem:** Colour maps that visually distort data through uneven colour gradients or are unreadable to those with colour-vision deficiency remain prevalent in science, including rainbow-like and red–green colour maps.

**Solutions Proposed:** Scientifically derived colour maps report true data variations, reduce complexity, and are accessible for people with colour-vision deficiencies. 

**Call to Action:** The authors highlight ways for the scientific community to identify and prevent the misuse of colour in science, and call for a proactive step away from colour misuse among the community, publishers, and the press.

The research specifically focuses on how improper use of colour in visualizations—particularly rainbow colormaps—can create visual artifacts and distort data representation in scientific communication.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

# Analysis of Rainbow Colormaps Research

**Author Note:** The paper is by Khairi Reda, not Ware et al.

## Full Abstract

"Guidelines for color use in quantitative visualizations have strongly discouraged the use of rainbow colormaps, arguing instead for smooth designs that do not induce visual discontinuities or implicit color categories. However, the empirical evidence behind this argument has been mixed and, at times, even contradictory. In practice, rainbow colormaps are widely used, raising questions about the true utility or dangers of such designs. We study how color categorization impacts the interpretation of scalar fields. We first introduce an approach to detect latent categories in colormaps. We hypothesize that the appearance of color categories in scalar visualizations can be beneficial in that they enhance the perception of certain features, although at the cost of rendering other features less noticeable. In three crowdsourced experiments, we show that observers are more likely to discriminate global, distributional features when viewing colorful scales that induce categorization (e.g., rainbow or diverging schemes). Conversely, when seeing the same data through a less colorful representation, observers are more likely to report localized features defined by small variations in the data. Participants showed awareness of these different affordances, and exhibited bias for exploiting the more discriminating colormap, given a particular feature type. Our results demonstrate costs and benefits for rainbows (and similarly colorful schemes), suggesting that their complementary utility for analyzing scalar data should not be dismissed. In addition to explaining potentially valid uses of rainbow, our study provides actionable guidelines, including on when such designs can be more harmful than useful."

## Key Findings

**Good for:** "Observers are more likely to discriminate global, distributional features when viewing colorful scales" (like rainbows).

**Bad for:** Detecting localized, small-scale variations in data.

**Additional note:** The abstract does not mention false features, artificial boundaries, or misreading maxima.

1. QUOTE-MISREAD ATTACK (the most likely kill, since the quote mentions "red-green colorblind"): FAILED. I fetched the PLOS ONE article to check whether panels (b) and (c) are BOTH CVD simulations — if so, the "without CVD" half of the claim would be unsupported. Figure 1 caption reads: "(a) perceptually uniform grayscale, (b) jet, (c) jet as it appears to someone with red-green colorblindness, and (d) viridis." Panel (b) is jet under NORMAL vision. The quoted passage says the bright yellow spots in (b) AND (c) "appear to represent significantly higher values than the surrounding regions. However, in fact, the dark red (in b) ... actually represent the highest values," then adds "For someone who is red-green colorblind, this is made even more difficult" — i.e. the paper explicitly frames CVD as an aggravating factor on top of a normal-vision failure, exactly as the claim states. Paper text also states problematic colormaps "can cause misinterpretation for certain types of data, even for those with normal color vision." The "AND without CVD" wording is supported, not overreach.

2. INDEPENDENT-CORROBORATION CHECK: the mechanism is not resting on one 2018 paper. Borland & Taylor, "Rainbow Color Map (Still) Considered Harmful," IEEE CG&A 27(2), 2007 (PMID 17388198): the rainbow "confuses viewers through its lack of perceptual ordering, obscures data through its uncontrolled luminance variation, and actively misleads interpretation through the introduction of non-data-dependent gradients" — "non-data-dependent gradients" is the same false-feature mechanism. Crameri, Shephard & Heron, Nature Communications 11:5444 (2020), "The misuse of colour in science communication," treats rainbow-induced visual distortion as an established defect. Jet's L* profile is non-monotonic (dark blue → bright yellow/cyan → dark red), so the bright band sitting at ~0.6-0.7 of the range while the maximum is dark red is a property of the colormap, not an interpretation.

3. CONTRADICTING-EVIDENCE SEARCH: I specifically hunted the revisionist literature. Two real dissents exist and NEITHER contradicts this claim. (a) Ware, Stone & Szafir, "Rainbow Colormaps Are Not All Bad," IEEE CG&A 43(3):88-93, 2023 — they CONCEDE the luminance defect verbatim ("it's not uniform in its luminance") and argue only about task relevance: "We understand well enough why rainbows can be bad; let us focus instead on finding out when and why they are good." (b) Reda, "Rainbow Colormaps: What are they good and bad for?", IEEE TVCG 2022 (PMID 36240035) — abstract says the empirical evidence has "been mixed and, at times, even contradictory," but its own finding is that rainbow "induce[s] categorization," which HELPS global/distributional feature discrimination and HURTS "localized features defined by small variations in the data." That is the false-boundary mechanism confirmed and merely re-scored as sometimes-useful. Both dispute the blanket prescription "never use rainbow"; neither disputes that the artifact exists.

4. DATE/QUALITY CHECK: PLOS ONE 2018, peer-reviewed, primary, not a press release or vendor content. Claim is reaffirmed by 2020 Nature Comms and conceded by the 2023 counter-paper, so not outdated. Claim strength (a specific, mechanistic, falsifiable failure mode) is matched by source quality.
